TextView.android:text: Teach it
When a commercial starts, press Is an ad. When your show is back, press Show\'s back. It remembers the whole break. Ducked your show by mistake? Not an ad.
Manual duck and remote
Turn the TV down for a fixed time, whatever the methods think, then back up on its own. Nothing is learned. The remote has every TV button plus all of this.
Test mode
Talks to the TV the way a commercial would: asks the volume, mutes and unmutes, ducks and restores. The sound should dip twice. Every byte is printed below.

TextView.android:text: Eight ways to spot a commercial
Switch on any mix. At least one must be on, or the app has nothing to go on and will not start. A coloured dot means that method is running right now.
1. Quiet gaps
The microphone hears the short silence broadcasters leave between the show and each commercial. A hint: needs another method to agree.
2. Loudness jumps
Commercials are mixed louder than the show. The microphone notices the sound jumping up and staying up. A hint: needs another method to agree.
3. Remembered breaks
Every break you bracket with Is an ad and Show\'s back is remembered as an audio fingerprint (numbers, not a recording) and recognised next time it airs. Strong enough to duck on its own.
4. Channel bug (camera)
The back camera watches the corner where the channel\'s logo — the bug — lives. Bug gone for 2.5 s means a commercial. Only acts while the whole TV is in view. Strong enough to duck on its own.
What to watch

TextView.android:text: 5. Spoken words (speech)
An offline speech recogniser turns what the microphone hears into words. Commercials repeat their words; the app saves them as scripts and recognises them. Strong enough to duck on its own.

com.google.android.material.radiobutton..android:text: Better model (128 MB, hears more over the fans)

TextView.android:text: 6. On-screen captions

With the TV\'s closed captions on, the camera reads the caption text off the screen and matches it to scripts like speech — but nothing is misheard over the fans. Needs the whole TV in view. Strong enough to duck on its own.

com.google.android.material.materialswit.android:text: Read the captions with the camera

TextView.android:text: 7. Ask Claude (cloud AI)

Sends the last 40 seconds of words to Claude and asks: is this a commercial? Needs Speech or Captions for the words, an API key, and Wi-Fi. Costs about 13 cents an hour of TV with Haiku; a tenth of that as a tie-breaker. Only text leaves the phone.

TextView.android:text: 8. Local AI (on the phone)

The same question answered by a language model on the phone (Qwen, downloaded once). Free, private, no Wi-Fi needed; a few seconds per answer and a warmer phone. Needs Speech or Captions for the words.

TextView.android:text: 9. Break clock

Learns which minutes of the hour the breaks land on, from every break the other methods or you confirm. Once a minute has been watched for three hours it votes; it tips the balance but never ducks alone.
10. Break jingles

The channel plays the same short sting into and out of every break. Every break the app ends teaches the seconds around its start and end; a sting that opens three breaks is promoted and from then on ducks the set the moment it plays, and its closing sting brings the show back. One fingerprint per channel instead of one per ad.

com.google.android.material.materialswit.android:text: Learn and recognise the break jingles

TextView.android:text: Learn from a stream

Play the channel\'s live stream on this phone (MS NOW, Xfinity Stream, any web player in Chrome) and the phone hears its own playback and learns every break into the same memory it uses at the TV. No TV is touched. Android 10 or newer; you will be asked to allow screen recording: the sound is what is learned from, and with the switch below on, the corners of the picture are read for the player\'s AD badge. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere.

com.google.android.material.materialswit.android:text: Read the player\'s AD badge off the screen (near-certain breaks)
